Helicobacter pylori eradication does not heal or prevent relapse of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease,1 and some epidemiological evidence has appeared to suggest that H. pylori infection protects against gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.13 However, there is no clinical evidence that erad- ication of H. pylori exacerbates gastro-oesophageal reflux disease or significantly increases the risk of its develop- ment.14,15 In patients who have a poor response to drug therapy, or in those with complications such as oesophageal stricture or ulceration, surgery to re-establish gastro-oesophageal competence may be considered.1,4,5 Submucosal implants and various other endoscopic techniques have also been investigated.4 Although surgery is as effective as drug treatment, it carries greater associated risks, and many pa- tients continue to require antisecretory drugs.4 Investigational approaches to drug therapy include the development of drugs with GABAergic actions similar to those of baclofen (but without its CNS effects), chole- cystokinin antagonists such as loxiglumide, and cannabi- noid CB1 agonists; motilin receptor agonists such as alem- cinal and mitemcinal do not appear to be of much benefit.16 A minority of patients with gastro-oesophageal reflux dis- ease develop Barrett’s oesophagus (columnar lined oesophagus, CLO), in which the normal oesophageal squamous lining is replaced with a metaplastic columnar epithelium. This is most common in patients with long- standing disease but may represent part of a spectrum of possible responses to acid reflux rather than a progression from less severe to more severe disease.4 The abnormal epithelium in Barrett’s oesophagus shows dysplastic changes that may progress to oesophageal adenocarcino- ma. However, not all patients go on to develop cancer, and many aspects of management are controversial. Management of acid reflux, as for other forms of gastro- oesophageal reflux disease, is the mainstay of manage- ment.17-20 Long-term treatment with PPIs appears to be ef- fective;19 the use of maximal doses, perhaps in combina- tion with an H2-antagonist at night, is advocated by some20 but evidence to support twice daily (double) dosing is lacking.19 As the altered epithelium is relatively less sensi- tive to acid, symptom control does not necessarily equate to suppression of reflux.20 There is a lack of good evidence that control of acid reflux produces anything other than limited regression of the abnormal epithelium, or alters the risk of progression to malignancy,19,20 although there are some results that suggest benefit.21,22 Some evidence sug- gest
